segments.Guide_for_the_Perplexed_Letter_to_R_Jose: In the name of the Lord, God of the World.
My dear student, Rabbi Joseph [may God preserve him], son of Rabbi Judah [may he rest in peace]:

When you stood before me, having come from the ends of the earth to study under my guidance, your stature grew in my eyes due to your great diligence in study, and because I recognized in your poems a profound desire for speculative matters. This was already evident from the letters and Maqamat you sent me from Alexandria, even before I had tested your capacity for comprehension. I said to myself: 'Perhaps his desire is greater than his grasp.' But when you studied under my direction what you have already studied of astronomy, and the mathematics necessary as a preparation for it which you had learned previously, my joy in you increased because of your sound intellect and the quickness of your perception. I saw that your passion for mathematics was great, and I allowed you to train in it, knowing where it would lead you. And when you studied under my direction what you have already studied of the science of logic, I placed my hopes in you, and found you worthy of having the secrets of the prophetic books revealed to you, so that you might understand from them what is fitting for perfect individuals to understand. Therefore, I began to hint and provide you with subtle indications. Then I saw you seeking more from me, and urging me to explain matters of the divine sciences, and to inform you of the intentions of the 'Mutakallimun' (theologians), and whether their methods are demonstrative, and if not—to which discipline they belong.

And when God decreed our separation and you turned to wherever you turned, these encounters moved me to a resolution that had previously weakened, and your absence prompted me to compose this work, which I have written for you and for those like you, few as they may be. I have arranged it in separate chapters, and each part that is written will reach you one by one wherever you may be, and may you be in peace.
segments.Guide_for_the_Perplexed_Prefatory_Remark: The primary purpose of this work is to explain the meanings of terms appearing in the books of prophecy. Some of these are equivocal terms, which the ignorant understand only in one of their several meanings. Others are metaphorical, which they also understand only in their primary sense. Still others are amphibolous (uncertain), which sometimes seem to be used univocally and sometimes equivocally.

The objective of this work is not to explain all of them to the masses, nor to beginners in speculation, nor to teach one whose only study has been the knowledge of the Torah—and I mean 'knowledge of the Torah' in its limited sense: its laws. For truly, the purpose of this entire work and all those of its kind is the knowledge of the Torah in its truth. Rather, the purpose of this work is to awaken a religious person whose soul has already established and attained in its faith the truth of our Torah, and who is perfect in his religion and character, and has studied the sciences of the philosophers and knows their meanings, and whose human intellect has drawn and led him to dwell in its palace, but who is held back by the literal meanings of the Scripture and what he understood or what others explained to him of these equivocal, metaphorical, or uncertain terms. Thus he remains perplexed and bewildered: either he follows his intellect and casts aside what he learned (erroneously) from these terms, thinking he is thereby casting aside religious foundations; or he stays with what he understood from them and does not follow his intellect, finding himself turning his back on his intellect and distancing himself from it. At the same time, he will think he has brought upon himself harm and injury to his religion (through his intellectual inquiry), and will remain with those imaginary beliefs, terrified and tormented by them, constantly dwelling in heartache and severe confusion.
